h1: Maltodextrin for body in low-alcohol beer
title: Maltodextrin for Low-Alcohol Body | Craft Beer School
desc: How maltodextrin adds body to low-alcohol and alcohol-free beer: dose, when to add it, what it does to gravity and the stability risks.
teaser: Low-alcohol beer often tastes watery. Maltodextrin is one of the cheapest fixes, as long as you know what it cannot do.
standfirst: Take alcohol out of a beer and you take body with it. Maltodextrin, an unfermentable carbohydrate, can put some of that mouthfeel back. It works best as one part of a recipe designed for low alcohol, not as a patch on a thin beer.
sections: Low-alcohol beer tastes thin because ethanol carries body

Ethanol does more than make a beer strong. It adds warmth, a touch of sweetness and viscosity. A 5% lager has about 40 g of alcohol per litre doing that work. Remove it, or never make it. The beer then feels watery even if the malt and hop flavour are right.

Brewers making beers under about 1% ABV have a few ways to rebuild body: a mash that leaves more dextrins, specialty malts, oats, protein for foam and added carbohydrates. Maltodextrin is the most direct of those. It is also the easiest to overdo.
Maltodextrin is a short chain of glucose that yeast leaves alone

Maltodextrin is made by partly breaking down starch, usually from maize, tapioca or potato. The product is sold by its dextrose equivalent (DE), a measure of how far the starch has been broken down. Brewing grades are typically under DE 20. At that range most of the chains are too long for brewing yeast to ferment.

So maltodextrin raises the original gravity and the final gravity by almost the same amount. As a rough guide, each gram per litre adds about 0.1 °P, roughly 0.4 gravity points. A 10 g/L dose lifts both gravities by about 1 °P. It adds little sweetness and almost no flavour, only a smoother, fuller texture.
Start at 5 to 10 grams per litre

Dosing depends on the beer and the base you start from. A common starting range is 5 to 10 g/L, which is 5 to 10 kg in a 1,000 litre batch. Below that the effect is hard to taste. Above about 15 g/L many tasters pick up a slick, starchy or slightly cardboard mouthfeel that reads as artificial.

Run a bench trial before you change a recipe. Dose four glasses of the finished beer at 0, 5, 10 and 15 g/L with a dissolved stock solution. Taste them blind with your team. You will usually find the point where the beer stops tasting watery well before the point where it tastes thick.
Add it after the mash, never during

The enzymes in a working mash will happily break maltodextrin down into fermentable sugar, which defeats the purpose. Add it in the last 10 to 15 minutes of the boil instead. Dissolve the powder in hot wort in a bucket first, because it clumps if tipped straight into the kettle.

Some brewers add it to the brite tank as a sterile syrup instead, which lets them adjust body after fermentation. That needs careful sanitation, since you are adding a carbohydrate to beer that may never be boiled again.
Residual carbohydrate makes low-alcohol beer easier to spoil

This is the floor detail that matters most. A normal beer is protected by alcohol, hop acids, low pH and a lack of sugar. A low-alcohol beer has lost the alcohol and often carries more residual carbohydrate. Maltodextrin adds to that.

Most spoilage bacteria do not ferment long dextrins easily, but some yeasts can. Saccharomyces cerevisiae var. diastaticus carries an enzyme that breaks dextrins down. In a sealed can that means slow refermentation, rising pressure and a risk of gushing or bursting. Low-alcohol beers in India face long warm journeys, so treat pasteurisation or sterile filtration as standard. Check pH at packaging too. Many brewers aim for 4.2 or below in low-alcohol beers.
It works best alongside other body builders

Maltodextrin alone can taste one-dimensional. The best low-alcohol beers stack small contributions:

  • A high saccharification rest around 72 °C to favour alpha-amylase and leave dextrins.
  • Dextrin malt, such as Weyermann CARAPILS, for body and foam.
  • Flaked oats at 5 to 10% for a silky texture. Our guide to oats in beer covers the lautering trade-off.
  • A maltose-negative yeast, which ferments only simple sugars and leaves maltose behind.

Each of these also changes flavour, foam and stability. Balancing them for a target ABV and gravity is a design job. It takes an understanding of mash enzymes and yeast metabolism that a dose chart cannot give you.

Maltodextrin is a food ingredient and should appear on your ingredient declaration. Check the current FSSAI labelling rules for alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages, which differ and change over time. Record lot numbers and dose rates in your batch log so you can trace any complaint.
Run a four-glass trial this week

Take your current low-alcohol beer and dose four samples at 0, 5, 10 and 15 g/L. Taste them blind with two colleagues. If the 5 or 10 g/L glass wins, you have a cheap improvement to scale. If none of them fix the thinness, the recipe needs work further upstream.
faqs: Normal brewing yeast ferments very little of it. Diastaticus strains can break dextrins down, which is a spoilage risk in packaged beer.
How much maltodextrin should I add to low-alcohol beer?
Start around 5 to 10 g/L and confirm with a blind bench trial. Above about 15 g/L many tasters notice a slick or starchy mouthfeel.
In the last 10 to 15 minutes of the boil, dissolved first. Adding it to the mash lets enzymes break it down into fermentable sugar.
Is maltodextrin enough on its own?
Rarely. It works best alongside a high mash temperature, dextrin malt, oats or a maltose-negative yeast.
